title: MDPs and POMDPs
summary: The decision model must distinguish the environment's state from the information available to the agent.

sections.title: What makes a state Markov?
paragraphs: A Markov decision process describes states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and an evaluation horizon or discount. Its state contains enough information that the next-state distribution depends on the current state and action rather than the entire past. This is a modeling assumption, not a statement that every camera image is a complete state. In robotics, hidden velocities, contacts, or occluded objects can make a single observation insufficient.

sections.title: Represent partial observability
paragraphs: A partially observable MDP adds an observation process. The agent receives o rather than the complete state s and may use a belief distribution b(s) or a learned memory of past observations. After an action and new observation, a Bayesian belief update combines the transition model with observation likelihood. For example, a drawer may look closed whether it is empty or contains a key; remembering an earlier insertion changes what the agent should believe.

sections.title: Match the policy input to the setting
paragraphs: A feedforward policy using one image implicitly relies on that image being sufficient for its task, or accepts the resulting ambiguity. Stacked frames can reveal motion, while recurrent models can integrate longer histories. Neither automatically recovers all hidden state. When comparing policies, declare whether privileged simulator state is available during training, evaluation, or only to a critic. Giving one policy hidden object coordinates while another sees RGB images creates a different information problem, even if both control the same robot.

exercise.prompt: Two visually identical observations have different object velocities and require different braking actions. Is the image alone necessarily a Markov state?
exercise.answer: No. If velocity affects the next state and appropriate action, the image omits relevant information. A history, velocity sensor, or belief representation may help distinguish the situations.

takeaways: Markov state and observed input are not interchangeable.
Declare privileged information explicitly.

title: Observations, States, Actions, and Trajectories
summary: A robotics dataset needs consistent semantics, timing, and units for every recorded signal.

sections.title: Name the quantities before modeling
paragraphs: An observation is what sensors or preprocessing expose to the policy, such as images and joint readings. State describes the environment variables relevant to dynamics. An action is a command interpreted by a controller or simulator. A trajectory is the time-ordered sequence linking these quantities and outcomes. Two datasets can both store a seven-dimensional action while meaning entirely different things: joint positions, joint velocities, or an end-effector pose plus gripper command.

sections.title: Align measurements with commands
paragraphs: Write a record as (ot,at,ot+1), but determine whether at was issued immediately after ot or reflects a delayed control signal. Camera exposure, transport, inference, and actuator execution all introduce timing offsets. An end-effector translation may be absolute or relative, expressed in world or tool coordinates, and measured in meters or another scale. Rotation representations also require explicit conventions. Normalization statistics should be fitted to training data and inverted correctly before execution.

sections.title: Inspect a trajectory end to end
paragraphs: Plot representative sensor channels and commanded actions against timestamps. Check episode boundaries, missing frames, action clipping, and whether gripper commands are continuous or discrete. Verify that a decoded action produces the intended movement in a controlled simulator example before interpreting policy quality. A model can achieve low prediction loss on misaligned data while issuing systematically late commands. Preserve dataset metadata with checkpoints so the exact observation preprocessing and action decoder are recoverable.

exercise.prompt: A predicted translation vector [0.01,0,0] is interpreted in the tool frame instead of the world frame. Why can the physical movement differ?
exercise.answer: The tool frame rotates with the end effector, while the world frame is fixed. The same numeric vector points in different world directions when the tool orientation changes; the coordinate convention is part of the action definition.

takeaways: Action dimensions do not specify action meaning.
Timing, coordinate frames, and units belong in the model contract.

title: Behavior Cloning and Imitation Learning
summary: Behavior cloning learns demonstrated actions, but deployment exposes the policy to states its own actions create.

sections.title: Treat demonstrations as supervision
paragraphs: Behavior cloning fits a policy to observation-action pairs collected from an expert or demonstration source. A discrete policy may minimize cross-entropy, while a continuous policy may minimize a regression or likelihood objective. Imitation learning is broader: it can include interactive data collection or other ways of using demonstrations. Behavior cloning does not require a reward model or an RL loop, which makes it a useful first baseline when demonstrations are available.

sections.title: Understand multimodal actions
paragraphs: At an obstacle, going left and going right may both be successful. A deterministic squared-error predictor trained on both can output their average, which points directly into the obstacle. A distributional action model can represent alternatives, although it still needs a reliable execution strategy. The training objective should reflect action units and scales; a large numeric position dimension can otherwise dominate a smaller but important gripper signal. Sequence context may disambiguate the demonstrator's intent.

sections.title: Evaluate closed-loop behavior
paragraphs: Held-out action prediction error measures agreement on recorded observations. It does not fully measure recovery when the learned policy drifts into unfamiliar states. Roll out the policy under controlled initial conditions, inspect failures, and compare against simple baselines. More diverse demonstrations or interactive expert corrections can improve coverage, but data access and collection costs should be reported. Separate demonstration quality from model capacity: imitating an inconsistent or poorly aligned dataset can preserve its mistakes efficiently.

exercise.prompt: Demonstrations choose action −1 or +1 equally often at the same observed state. What does a deterministic squared-error optimum predict?
exercise.answer: It predicts their conditional mean, 0. If zero is an invalid or unsafe middle path, low average regression loss does not imply useful behavior. A multimodal policy or additional context may be needed.

takeaways: Behavior cloning is supervised learning on demonstrations.
Prediction accuracy on expert states is not closed-loop success.

title: Action Chunking and ACT
summary: Predicting a short sequence of actions can capture temporal structure while reducing repeated policy inference.

sections.title: Predict more than one command
paragraphs: An action-chunk policy maps recent observations to a horizon of H future actions, often represented as [B,H,Da] for batch size B and action dimension Da. The chunk models short temporal coordination, such as approaching an object and closing a gripper. ACT is a concrete action-chunking approach using a Transformer-based policy. Chunking is an interface choice: different generative models can produce the sequence, and execution need not consume the entire chunk.

sections.title: Separate prediction from execution
paragraphs: Suppose a policy predicts 20 actions but executes only the first 5 before observing again. The remaining actions serve as planned context and may be replaced during replanning. Overlapping predictions for the same future time can be combined through temporal aggregation, provided their timestamps and action semantics align. This can smooth commands, but averaging is not always appropriate when predictions represent incompatible modes. A chunk's horizon should be interpreted in seconds as well as step count.

sections.title: Balance coherence and responsiveness
paragraphs: Longer chunks reduce how frequently expensive inference is required and can preserve motion consistency. They also risk acting on stale observations if executed without feedback. A short action horizon can respond quickly but increase compute demand and discontinuity between plans. Report predicted horizon, executed horizon, control rate, observation history, and aggregation rule. Evaluate disturbances occurring mid-chunk rather than only nominal demonstrations. Do not attribute every improvement to chunking when the comparison also changes model size or demonstration coverage.

exercise.prompt: A policy predicts 30 actions at 20 Hz and executes 6 before replanning. What are the prediction and execution horizons?
exercise.answer: The predicted horizon is 30/20=1.5 seconds, and the executed open-loop portion is 6/20=0.3 seconds. New observations can influence the next plan after that execution interval, subject to system latency.

takeaways: Predicted horizon and executed horizon are separate settings.
Chunking trades inference frequency against feedback freshness.

title: Diffusion and Flow-Based Action Policies
summary: Generative action policies model distributions over coordinated continuous action sequences.

sections.title: Generate a trajectory in action space
paragraphs: Instead of predicting one deterministic action vector, a generative policy samples an action sequence conditioned on observations and possibly language. This can represent multiple valid behaviors, such as approaching an object from different sides. Diffusion policies learn to reverse a noise process on action sequences. Flow-based policies learn a velocity field that transports an initial distribution toward the action distribution. Both need a decoder from normalized model outputs to meaningful robot commands.

sections.title: Trace the conditional computation
paragraphs: For a horizon H and action dimension Da, the sample can have shape [H,Da]. A diffusion model receives a noisy version, a noise-level indicator, and observation features, then predicts a quantity used by the chosen denoising update. A flow model predicts vθ(xt,t,o) and integrates an update such as xt+Δt≈xt+Δt vθ(xt,t,o). This Euler expression illustrates numerical integration, not a claim that every implementation uses one step or the same path.

sections.title: Account for sampling and control
paragraphs: Multiple generation steps add inference latency, which matters when the robot must react quickly. Fewer steps can change sample quality, so compare success and wall-clock delay together. Use a receding-horizon execution policy and measure robustness to disturbances. Training-time action normalization, observation conditioning, and horizon masks must match inference. A smooth sampled sequence is not automatically dynamically feasible; the controller and action limits still determine what is executed. Evaluate diversity through successful alternatives rather than merely noisy command variation.

exercise.prompt: Why can a model with excellent offline denoising loss still perform poorly in closed-loop control?
exercise.answer: Its samples may arrive too late, visit unfamiliar states, violate action conventions, or fail to recover from disturbances. The denoising objective measures one component of the system, while control success depends on the whole observation-generation-execution loop.

takeaways: Generative action quality must be evaluated through execution.
Sampling latency is part of the policy design.

title: Vision-Language-Action Architectures
summary: A VLA model connects visual observations and language goals to an explicit robot action representation.

sections.title: Ground words in executable behavior
paragraphs: A vision-language model can describe a scene without controlling it. A vision-language-action model additionally maps observations and instructions to actions interpreted by a robot or simulator. The instruction may specify which object to manipulate or which goal to achieve. Visual understanding helps locate relevant evidence, but action grounding requires information about embodiment, control conventions, and task dynamics. A correct verbal description does not guarantee a useful command.

sections.title: Follow the interface
paragraphs: A visual encoder produces features, language tokens represent the instruction, and a fusion or language-model component combines them. An action head or token decoder produces commands. Some systems discretize actions into tokens and predict them autoregressively; others use continuous heads, diffusion, or flow. RT-2 is an example of connecting vision-language learning with tokenized robot actions. The action decoder must specify dimensions, units, coordinate frames, and how special symbols map to termination or gripper behavior.

sections.title: Test grounding rather than vocabulary
paragraphs: Use instructions that distinguish similar objects, change spatial relations, or require different actions in the same scene. Evaluate whether language actually affects behavior by comparing controlled instruction changes. Report the embodiment and action space; transferring semantic knowledge does not automatically transfer motor control across robots. Separate pretrained visual-language capability from robot demonstration data and any additional adaptation. Failure analysis should distinguish perception errors, instruction misunderstanding, invalid action decoding, timing problems, and physical execution failures.

exercise.prompt: A system answers 'pick up the blue cup' correctly in text but outputs joint commands for a different robot layout. Is the task solved?
exercise.answer: No. The action representation is incompatible with the execution interface. Semantic understanding must be connected to the correct embodiment, joint ordering, units, and controller for the behavior to succeed.

takeaways: Language understanding and action grounding are distinct.
The action interface is part of the architecture.

title: Autoregressive and Continuous Action Generation
summary: Output factorization and action representation are separate design axes rather than mutually exclusive model families.

sections.title: Separate two questions
paragraphs: Autoregressive generation predicts components sequentially, conditioning each on earlier outputs. Continuous representation describes actions as real-valued quantities rather than discrete symbols. A model can be autoregressive over continuous actions, or jointly generate a horizon of discretized actions. Treating 'autoregressive versus continuous' as a strict binary hides this distinction. Also separate generation order from execution order: a full action sequence can be generated before any command is executed.

sections.title: Compare representative implementations
paragraphs: A token policy may quantize each action dimension into bins and predict a sequence of bin IDs. This reuses categorical likelihood machinery but introduces discretization resolution and potentially many decoding steps. A continuous regression head outputs values directly, while diffusion or flow models can generate an entire action chunk through iterative refinement. Each method has different latency, multimodality, and likelihood properties. A finer bin grid reduces quantization error but increases vocabulary or sequence complexity depending on encoding.

sections.title: Measure the actual trade-offs
paragraphs: Compare success under a shared control interface and include decoding latency, action precision, and invalid-output handling. Quantized actions can be adequate if the controller tolerates their resolution; continuous values can still be poorly calibrated or out of bounds. Autoregressive factorization may capture dependencies but accumulate earlier output errors. Joint prediction can model coordination while requiring its own mechanism for diverse alternatives. State what is sequential: tokens, action dimensions, timesteps, or denoising iterations.

exercise.prompt: A Gaussian policy predicts one continuous action at each timestep conditioned on previous actions. Is it autoregressive or continuous?
exercise.answer: It is both. Its outputs are continuous, and its temporal factorization is autoregressive. These labels describe different properties and should not be used as exclusive categories.

takeaways: Representation and factorization are independent choices.
Compare executable precision and latency, not labels alone.

title: Closed-Loop Control and Replanning
summary: Repeated observation lets a policy correct errors before they compound across an entire planned trajectory.

sections.title: Use feedback after acting
paragraphs: An open-loop controller commits to commands without incorporating new observations during execution. A closed-loop controller observes the resulting state or signals and adjusts subsequent actions. Replanning is one way to use feedback: predict a future action sequence, execute a prefix, observe again, and generate a new sequence. This can correct unexpected object motion, imperfect actuation, or prediction error, provided sensing and inference are fast enough.

sections.title: Trace receding-horizon execution
paragraphs: Suppose a policy predicts ten actions but executes two before updating. The unexecuted eight actions are tentative and can be replaced. The policy may use them as a warm start, but it should not treat predicted observations as if they were measured. Feedback has a delay from sensing, transport, inference, and command scheduling. Even a nominally closed-loop system can behave nearly open-loop during a disturbance if that total delay is long relative to the dynamics.

sections.title: Evaluate recovery explicitly
paragraphs: Test perturbations such as shifted object positions or delayed observations within a controlled simulation protocol. Record response time, overshoot, and final success rather than only smoothness. Replanning more often can increase compute demand or introduce jitter when consecutive predictions disagree. Use consistent action bounds and timing conventions when comparing policies. A successful nominal rollout does not establish robustness, and a failure does not always imply a poor high-level plan; the feedback loop may be using stale or misaligned measurements.

exercise.prompt: A policy replans every 50 ms but its observations are delayed by 500 ms. Is its feedback effectively fresh?
exercise.answer: No. Frequent replanning does not remove the observation delay. The policy repeatedly updates using old information, which can cause lag or inappropriate corrections in a fast-changing environment.

takeaways: Feedback usefulness depends on total delay.
Evaluate recovery from disturbances, not only nominal execution.

title: Synchronous and Asynchronous Policy Execution
summary: Overlapping inference with action execution can reduce waiting while creating challenges around stale plans and timing.

sections.title: Two scheduling patterns
paragraphs: A synchronous loop observes, computes a new action chunk, executes it, and repeats in a coordinated sequence. Depending on implementation, the robot may wait or hold its previous command while inference runs. An asynchronous loop can execute part of an existing plan while another process generates the next plan. This overlap can improve continuity, but the new prediction may be based on an observation that is already old when its first action is used.

sections.title: Align plans to execution time
paragraphs: If inference takes 120 ms and control runs at 20 Hz, more than two control intervals pass during generation. The new chunk's early actions may refer to times that have already elapsed. A system must decide how to skip, align, condition, or otherwise reconcile those actions with commands already executed. Timestamps and buffered action indices are therefore essential. Simply starting the new chunk at its first element can cause discontinuities or repeat movements intended for an earlier state.

sections.title: Measure freshness and continuity
paragraphs: Report observation age at action execution, queue depth, inference latency distribution, and behavior when generation misses its deadline. Compare schedules under the same policy and controller before attributing gains to model quality. Asynchrony does not guarantee lower end-to-end error; stale information can outweigh reduced idle time. Test varying compute load and disturbances during generation. The policy, scheduler, and low-level controller form one system, so inspect their interaction rather than benchmarking the neural network in isolation.

exercise.prompt: An action chunk is predicted from a frame captured 200 ms ago. Does zero queueing after inference make that frame current?
exercise.answer: No. The observation is still at least 200 ms old, plus any remaining transport or scheduling delay. Queueing is only one component of observation-to-action latency.

takeaways: Overlap reduces waiting but does not erase staleness.
Align generated actions with actual execution timestamps.

title: Compounding Errors and Distribution Shift
summary: Small imitation errors can push a policy into states that were rare in its demonstrations.

sections.title: The policy changes its own inputs
paragraphs: A supervised action predictor is usually trained on expert-visited observations. During rollout, its actions influence which observations arrive next. A small steering error may put a robot beside the path, where the expert dataset contains few recovery examples. Prediction quality can then degrade further, causing additional drift. This feedback between errors and visited states is why low held-out action loss does not automatically imply a successful long trajectory.

sections.title: Follow an unfamiliar state
paragraphs: Imagine demonstrations approach a cup from directly above. The learned policy approaches slightly sideways and sees an occlusion pattern absent from training. Continuing the nominal grasp command may worsen the misalignment. More examples of the original centered approach do not necessarily teach recovery from the side. Interactive imitation methods can collect expert guidance on learner-visited states, improving coverage of the distribution induced by the learner rather than only the original demonstration distribution.

sections.title: Separate the possible remedies
paragraphs: Data aggregation, disturbance augmentation, better observation history, and closed-loop correction target different parts of the problem. Their benefits depend on whether the augmented states and labels are realistic and relevant. Report additional expert queries and collection costs. Evaluate success as the horizon increases and inspect the first divergence, not only the final failure. Avoid universal linear or quadratic error-growth claims without stating the assumptions of the underlying analysis; actual dynamics, feedback, and recovery ability determine how errors propagate.

exercise.prompt: Why might doubling demonstrations of perfect centered grasps fail to fix sideways recovery?
exercise.answer: The added data can remain concentrated on the same expert-state distribution. If sideways states and appropriate corrective actions are still absent, the policy receives little direct supervision for recovery after its own deviation.

takeaways: Rollout errors alter the future input distribution.
Coverage of recovery states matters as well as dataset size.

title: World Models and Latent Dynamics
summary: A learned dynamics model predicts how internal state representations evolve and supports decisions through imagined outcomes.

sections.title: Model consequences, not only appearances
paragraphs: A world model approximates aspects of how an environment changes under actions. It may predict observations, rewards, termination, or a latent state that supports those predictions. Latent dynamics operate in a compressed representation rather than directly over every pixel. The representation should retain information relevant to future transitions and decisions. A visually attractive video predictor can still be a poor control model if it ignores action effects or important hidden variables.

sections.title: Trace an imagined rollout
paragraphs: An encoder infers latent state zt from observations and history. A dynamics model predicts zt+1 from zt and at, possibly stochastically. Additional heads predict rewards or reconstructed observations. Repeating these transitions yields an imagined trajectory used for planning or policy learning. For example, an agent can compare moving left and right without executing both in the real environment. The usefulness of that comparison depends on how accurate and calibrated the model is in the states and actions considered.

sections.title: Watch model exploitation
paragraphs: Planning can seek trajectories where the learned model is overly optimistic, especially outside its training distribution. Errors compound over imagined steps, and a small one-step prediction loss does not guarantee accurate long-horizon decisions. Evaluate action-conditioned predictions and downstream control separately. Ensembles, uncertainty estimates, short planning horizons, and fresh observations can help manage errors, but none guarantees correctness. Distinguish imagination used to train a policy from online model-predictive planning; both use a model but have different execution costs.

exercise.prompt: A model predicts future frames well when the robot stays still but ignores the action input. Why is it insufficient for planning?
exercise.answer: Planning compares the consequences of different actions. If predictions do not respond appropriately to actions, the model cannot rank those alternatives reliably, even when passive visual prediction looks accurate.

takeaways: Control requires action-sensitive predictive representations.
Imagined success is only as reliable as the learned dynamics.

title: Planning and Model Predictive Control
summary: MPC repeatedly optimizes a finite-horizon action plan and executes only its first part before observing again.

sections.title: Separate a policy from a planner
paragraphs: A policy directly maps available information to an action or action distribution. A planner evaluates candidate future action sequences using a model and objective. Model predictive control performs this planning repeatedly as new measurements arrive. The finite planning horizon makes the computation manageable, while replanning corrects deviations. MPC is therefore a feedback architecture, not a guarantee that the learned dynamics or objective faithfully capture the task.

sections.title: Write the optimization problem
paragraphs: At time t, choose actions a0:H−1 to minimize a predicted cost Σk c(zk,ak)+cfinal(zH), subject to modeled dynamics and any represented constraints. Execute the first action or short prefix, then solve again from the updated state estimate. Candidates can be optimized by gradients, sampling, or methods such as the cross-entropy method. In a simple reaching task, costs might combine distance to a target, excessive action magnitude, and predicted collisions.

sections.title: Inspect horizon and model errors
paragraphs: A short horizon can miss delayed consequences, while a long horizon increases compute and exposes more accumulated model error. Constraints enforced only in an inaccurate model may fail in the actual environment. Compare planners under equal sampling budgets and include online optimization time. Warm-starting from the previous plan can reduce computation but should not prevent adaptation to new evidence. Evaluate whether improvements come from a better dynamics model, a better optimizer, or a different cost function by varying these components separately.

exercise.prompt: Why does MPC normally discard or revise unexecuted actions instead of committing to the entire optimized sequence?
exercise.answer: New observations reveal disturbances and prediction errors. Replanning from that updated information can correct the remaining sequence; committing to the original plan would remove much of the feedback benefit.

takeaways: MPC optimizes repeatedly rather than trusting one complete plan.
Planning quality depends on model, cost, and compute budget.

title: Robotics Simulation and Benchmarks Such as LIBERO
summary: A benchmark defines a controlled task distribution and protocol, not a universal measure of robot intelligence.

sections.title: Know what the environment supplies
paragraphs: Simulation makes repeated resets, controlled perturbations, and large-scale evaluation easier. It also introduces assumptions about geometry, contact, sensing, and dynamics. A benchmark packages tasks, observations, action interfaces, and success conditions to make comparisons reproducible. LIBERO is an example centered on learning and transfer across manipulation tasks. Performance within one suite should be interpreted relative to its task distribution and protocol rather than as an unrestricted real-world capability claim.

sections.title: Read the protocol before the score
paragraphs: Identify task splits, demonstration counts, image views, action conventions, episode horizons, and reset distributions. Determine whether object arrangements or language instructions overlap across training and evaluation. A method given privileged simulator state is not directly comparable to an image-only method unless that difference is explicit. Check whether evaluation includes adaptation, additional demonstrations, or fine-tuning on test tasks; these change the learning problem and resource budget.

sections.title: Make the experiment reproducible
paragraphs: Record simulator and asset versions, environment wrappers, random seeds, and policy preprocessing. Save rollout videos and machine-readable outcomes so failures can be inspected. Evaluate multiple initial conditions and tasks rather than selecting a few attractive demonstrations. Simulator success may not transfer to hardware because friction, delays, camera calibration, and contact dynamics differ. Treat domain randomization or real-data adaptation as additional methods with measurable costs, and report which shifts were actually tested instead of assuming simulation diversity covers all deployment conditions.

exercise.prompt: Two policies report the same benchmark name, but one uses object poses and the other only RGB images. Are their scores automatically comparable?
exercise.answer: No. They solve different observation problems. The comparison must disclose the information available to each policy and ideally include matched-input baselines before attributing a score difference to architecture quality.

takeaways: A benchmark score is conditional on its full protocol.
Simulation transfer requires separate evidence.

references.title: LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning
references.note: Inspect task suites, demonstrations, and evaluation protocols.

title: Success Rates, Rollouts, and Failure Diagnosis
summary: Reliable evaluation combines repeated task outcomes with evidence about where and why a policy fails.

sections.title: Define success before collecting results
paragraphs: A rollout is one execution from an initial condition under a policy and termination rule. Success rate is the fraction satisfying a declared criterion. That criterion might require an object to remain in a target region for a specified duration, not merely pass through it once. Episode length, retries, intervention rules, and timeout handling can all change the measured rate. Freeze these choices before comparing methods.

sections.title: Count trials at the right level
paragraphs: With k successes in n trials, the observed rate is k/n. Uncertainty depends on the number and dependence structure of trials. Repeating the same deterministic initial condition does not provide the same evidence as sampling diverse task instances. Aggregate results by task as well as overall, since a large number of easy trials can hide poor performance on difficult tasks. Paired initial conditions can make policy comparisons more informative, provided the protocol remains consistent.

sections.title: Diagnose the first meaningful failure
paragraphs: Review videos and logs to separate perception, instruction interpretation, action decoding, timing, contact, and recovery failures. The final visible error may be a consequence of an earlier deviation. Record intervention and invalid-command rates, not only completed successes. A polished highlight reel cannot replace the denominator of all attempted rollouts. Report confidence intervals or another appropriate uncertainty summary, and keep test conditions separate from those used to tune thresholds or select checkpoints.

exercise.prompt: A policy succeeds in 18 of 20 trials, but three failed attempts were discarded because the robot timed out. What denominator should the declared protocol normally use?
exercise.answer: If timeouts are legitimate policy failures under the preset protocol, all 23 attempts belong in the denominator, giving 18/23. Excluding them after seeing outcomes inflates success and changes the evaluation definition.

takeaways: Declare success, timeout, and intervention rules in advance.
Inspect failure causes and preserve the full trial denominator.
